title: Restraining the Optimism That Leads to the Planning Fallacy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post addresses why projects nearly always take longer than planned: leaders underestimate time and resources, a bias known as the Planning Fallacy. The author frames resisting this optimism as essential work for good leaders, who prefer to underpromise and overdeliver. He argues that simply being realistic or consulting past projects is not enough. Instead, leaders should brainstorm obstacles with the team during planning so everyone counters the bias in their own work. They should also set contingency plans for missed deadlines, especially on high-stakes projects where failure would be catastrophic.
points: Leaders routinely underestimate complex projects because they stay optimistic about what can be done in the time allotted.
Being realistic or consulting prior projects does not offset the Planning Fallacy by itself.
Brainstorming potential obstacles with the team helps everyone combat the bias.
Contingency plans for missed deadlines prepare for the worst and underline the cost of unrealistic planning.
quotes: Leaders generally underestimate the time it will take to complete any complex task. They fail to account for the challenges and obstacles inherent in completing large or elaborate projects, preferring instead to remain optimistic about what could be achieved in the allotted time.

Underestimating the time and resources it takes to complete a project, known as the Planning Fallacy, is a common bias that inflicts almost everyone at one time or another. This bias can be both costly and wasteful as deadlines are shattered and budgets expanded to meet the project goals.

Simply being more realistic and using previous projects as a guide is not enough to offset this fallacy. Good leaders go out of their way in the planning process to brainstorm the potential obstacles and challenges that may derail execution.

Smart leaders also put contingency plans in place in the event that a project requires more time and resources. Knowing precisely how the team will handle missed deadlines and cost overrides not only prepares for the worst, but also drives home the point about the consequences of being unrealistic.
When it comes to underestimating what it takes to complete a complicated project, never undervalue the power of brainstorming what can get in the way.
